title: Implementation, Monitoring, and Learning
text:
Building from Monday
Monday: Evidence and framing shape a management plan.
Today: Implementation, monitoring, and evaluation show whether that plan works.

Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, §§6.3.3–6.3.4. Retrieve Plan–Do–Learn and ask students what could go wrong after a plan is adopted.


Source: Chapter 6, §§6.3.3–6.3.4

title: Implementation, Monitoring, and Learning
text:
The central question

How can managers learn whether an action produced both ecological and human benefits?


They need clear objectives, suitable measures, and a willingness to adapt.


Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, §§6.3.3–6.3.4.2.


Source: Chapter 6, §§6.3.3–6.3.4.2

title: Implementation, Monitoring, and Learning
text:
From plan to action
Implementation is where a plan meets real conditions.

Time: 1 minute. Transition slide.

title: Implementation, Monitoring, and Learning
section: Doing is more than announcing a plan

title: Implementation, Monitoring, and Learning
section: Plan–Do–Learn: each stage asks a different question
text:
Plan–Do–Learn: each stage asks a different question


Plan
What is the problem? What outcomes and alternatives matter?

Do
What action will be carried out, by whom, and under what constraints?

Learn
What changed? What should be adjusted next?


The cycle is not complete unless learning informs the next decision.


Time: 6 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, §6.3 and Figure 6.1. Invite students to trace one management decision through all three stages.


Source: Chapter 6, §6.3 and Figure 6.1

title: Implementation, Monitoring, and Learning
text:
Monitoring and evaluation
Evidence for learning rather than evidence for its own sake.

Time: 1 minute. Transition slide.

title: Implementation, Monitoring, and Learning
text:
Monitoring and evaluation are linked


Monitoring
Systematically and repeatedly collects information to guide future decisions.

Evaluation
Determines whether goals, objectives, and success measures were met.


Monitoring supplies evidence; evaluation interprets it against the decision’s objectives.


Time: 6 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, §§6.3.4–6.3.4.2. Ask why managers cannot use the terms as synonyms.


Source: Chapter 6, §§6.3.4–6.3.4.2

title: Implementation, Monitoring, and Learning
text:
Measures should match the objective


Ecological measures

population or habitat indicators
harvest levels
other resource conditions


Human-dimensions measures

support and satisfaction
license sales or days afield
perceptions of fairness or access



An evidence-informed decision can require both kinds of measures.


Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, §6.3.2.2. These are examples from the chapter, not a universal checklist.


Source: Chapter 6, §6.3.2.2

title: Implementation, Monitoring, and Learning
text:
What will count as success?
Before collecting data, managers need to decide:

What change is expected?
For whom should that change matter?
What evidence would show progress or a problem?
What decision could change in response?


Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, §§6.3.2–6.3.4. This slide synthesizes the chapter’s planning and learning logic. Ask students which question is hardest to answer before implementation begins.


Source: Chapter 6, §§6.3.2–6.3.4

title: Implementation, Monitoring, and Learning
text:
Chapter application: Puget Sound
The Puget Sound recovery effort combines ecological indicators with Human Well-being Vital Signs.

The effort involves agencies, Tribes, universities, practitioners, and other partners across the region.


Its measures help partners see whether recovery is affecting people as well as ecological conditions.


Time: 6 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, Box 6.2. Keep claims within the box; this is the shared case for Friday.


Source: Chapter 6, Box 6.2

title: Implementation, Monitoring, and Learning
text:
Human Well-being Vital Signs



air quality and drinking water
local foods and outdoor activity
cultural well-being
economic vitality



good governance
sense of place
stewardship behaviors



One indicator is not the whole story. Together, they broaden what recovery can mean.


Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, Box 6.2. Ask pairs to select one indicator and explain why it belongs in a recovery effort.


Source: Chapter 6, Box 6.2

title: Implementation, Monitoring, and Learning
section: Learning can change the next plan
text:
Learning can change the next plan


New evidence may change the problem frame, objectives, implementation, or measures—not simply confirm the original plan.


Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, §6.3.4 and Box 6.2. Explain the diagram in words. The alt text provides the text equivalent.


Source: Chapter 6, §6.3.4 and Box 6.2

title: Implementation, Monitoring, and Learning
text:
Friday: Puget Sound application
Prepare to explain:

the effort’s why, who, what, and how;
one Human Well-being Vital Sign and its relevance;
one implementation or coordination feature; and
how monitoring could guide the next planning cycle.


Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, Box 6.2. Pair students to locate direct support in the box. Remind them that the next reading quiz is due Sunday night before Monday’s class.


Source: Chapter 6, Box 6.2

title: Implementation, Monitoring, and Learning
section: Close: what counts as a strong decision?
text:
Close: what counts as a strong decision?
An evidence-informed decision is transparent about:

its objectives;
the evidence and values it uses;
implementation constraints; and
the ecological and human outcomes it will monitor.


Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, §§6.2–6.4. Close the week with the idea that learning is part of management, not a final add-on.


Source: Chapter 6, §§6.2–6.4

title: Justice, Participation, and Governance
text:
This week begins Wednesday
Monday is Labor Day. Today integrates Chapters 4 and 5 to prepare for Friday’s application.

Time: 2 minutes. Confirm that the quiz is due Tuesday at 11:59 p.m., before Wednesday’s class, because Monday is Labor Day.

title: Justice, Participation, and Governance
text:
Today’s question
How do equity, inclusion, justice, and governance shape whether a conservation decision is legitimate and durable?

Source: Chapter 4, §4.1–4.2; Chapter 5, §5.1–5.2.


Time: 3 minutes. Position the topics as integral to management practice.

title: Justice, Participation, and Governance
section: What you should be able to do
text:
What you should be able to do
By the end of today, you should be able to:

identify how access, recognition, participation, and influence affect a decision;
distinguish governance from a single agency’s day-to-day action; and
propose one accountable process that could strengthen the durability of a conservation decision.


Source: Chapters 4–5, §§4.1–4.2 and §§5.1–5.3.


Time: 2 minutes. Explain that Friday asks students to make both a justice and a governance claim using the same case.

title: Justice, Participation, and Governance
text:
Justice is a management condition
Access, influence, and recognition shape whether a conservation decision can be publicly legitimate.

Time: 1 minute. Do not present DEIJ as separate from ecological outcomes or implementation.

title: Justice, Participation, and Governance
section: DEIJ is part of management practice
text:
DEIJ is part of management practice
DEIJ shapes:

access to land and water;
whose knowledge is recognized;
who bears costs and receives benefits; and
who has influence in public processes.


Source: Chapter 4, §4.2.


Time: 6 minutes. Do not reduce DEIJ to representation alone. Ask students what each bullet means in a decision context.

title: Justice, Participation, and Governance
section: Why DEIJ matters to the profession
text:
Why DEIJ matters to the profession
DEIJ has three practical implications for the profession:

capacity: who enters, stays, and leads in the profession;
representation: whether the profession reflects the publics it serves; and
relevancy: whether conservation institutions can respond to changing communities, values, and relationships with nature.


Source: Chapter 4, §§4.3.1–4.3.3.


Time: 3 minutes. Avoid treating these as recruitment-only questions. Professional composition and institutional culture affect the ability to recognize problems, build relationships, and act effectively.

title: Justice, Participation, and Governance
text:
Four related terms

Diversity: varying attributes within a community.
Equity: fair opportunity to engage and benefit, including attention to barriers.
Inclusion: being accepted, supported, and able to contribute.
Justice: fair practices that dismantle barriers and enable full participation.


Source: Chapter 4, Table 4.1.


Time: 7 minutes. This is a concise text equivalent for Table 4.1. Ask students to distinguish equity from equality using only the table’s definitions.

title: Justice, Participation, and Governance
section: A process can include people without sharing influence
text:
A process can include people without sharing influence


Presence only
People are invited, but barriers limit their participation or their knowledge has no effect on the decision.

Meaningful inclusion
Relevant publics can participate, their knowledge is recognized, and the process makes clear how their input can affect the decision.


Source: Chapter 4, §§4.2–4.3.


Time: 4 minutes. Ask: “What would make an invitation insufficient?” Listen for access barriers, token participation, recognition, and a lack of meaningful influence. Do not require personal disclosure.

title: Justice, Participation, and Governance
section: Participation has to be designed, not announced
text:
Participation has to be designed, not announced
Meaningful participation requires more than an open meeting.

Identify affected publics and barriers to access.
Engage early enough for input to shape the problem and alternatives.
Explain the scope of influence and how input was used.
Build collaboration and accountability into the continuing relationship.


Source: Chapter 4, §4.4.2.


Time: 3 minutes. This provides a concrete bridge from terms to process. Be clear that meaningful participation does not mean every participant receives the outcome they prefer.

title: Justice, Participation, and Governance
text:
Governance makes process consequential
Rules, institutions, and power determine who can decide, implement, enforce, and participate.

Time: 1 minute. Bridge from justice concerns to the mechanisms that can either reproduce or address them.

title: Justice, Participation, and Governance
text:
Governance turns commitments into action
Governance is the interplay of rules, policies, institutions, and powers that guide decision-making, implementation, and enforcement.

Use this governance model to identify:

decision-making;
implementation; and
enforcement.


Source: Chapter 5, §5.2.


Time: 6 minutes. Use the figure’s alt text as the text equivalent. Emphasize that this Idaho figure is an example, not a universal structure; governance determines what actions are allowed, expected, and feasible.

title: Justice, Participation, and Governance
section: Governance rests on competing but connected principles
text:
Governance rests on competing but connected principles
Several governance foundations can pull a decision in different directions:

deliberative democracy;
public trust thinking;
sustainable use; and
the precautionary principle.


Governance is not only a chart of authority. It is also the principles used to justify how authority is exercised.


Source: Chapter 5, §§5.3.1–5.3.1.4.


Time: 3 minutes. Invite students to notice potential tensions: a decision can seek participation, public benefit, sustainable use, and caution under uncertainty at the same time.

title: Justice, Participation, and Governance
text:
Governance asks four practical questions

Authority: Who can make or change the decision?
Implementation: Who has to carry it out?
Accountability: Who can evaluate or challenge the decision?
Relationships: Which governments, publics, and partners must be involved for the decision to work?


Source: Chapter 5, §§5.2–5.3.


Time: 4 minutes. Use these as a checklist, not a claim that every decision has the same answer.

title: Justice, Participation, and Governance
section: Good governance is more than biological success
text:
Good governance is more than biological success
Good governance is transparent, inclusive, accountable, sustainable, adaptable, and capable of coordination across boundaries.

Source: Chapter 5, §5.3.2–5.3.3.


Time: 6 minutes. Ask students to identify which of these qualities would be hardest to assess and why.

title: Justice, Participation, and Governance
section: Funding is also a governance mechanism
text:
Funding is also a governance mechanism
Funding shapes what agencies can do, who they answer to, and which conservation work is feasible.

Federal excise-tax programs support state fish and wildlife work.
State, Tribal, Canadian, nongovernmental, and mitigation sources create additional pathways.
Diverse revenue can expand capacity, while each source can also bring constraints and expectations.


Source: Chapter 5, §5.6.


Time: 3 minutes. Link this back to the funding legacy discussed last week. The point is not that one source is inherently good or bad; it is that funding is part of governance and affects capacity and accountability.

title: Justice, Participation, and Governance
text:
Working across knowledge traditions


Source: Chapter 4, Figure 4.1.


Time: 5 minutes. Use this figure to deepen the DEIJ discussion. Ask students which principle is most relevant to meaningful participation and why.

title: Justice, Participation, and Governance
section: Work across knowledge traditions with humility
text:
Work across knowledge traditions with humility
Work across knowledge traditions by:

identify whose work and knowledge they are building on;
recognize the limits of their expertise;
understand that knowledge is positional; and
balance inquiry with practice.


Source: Chapter 4, §4.5.2 and Figure 4.1.


Time: 2 minutes. This text slide reinforces the figure rather than placing essential content only in an image. It is a practice standard, not an invitation to treat all knowledge claims as interchangeable.

title: Justice, Participation, and Governance
text:
Chapter application: Grand Staircase–Escalante
Grand Staircase–Escalante became a flashpoint when many local communities and Indigenous nations felt insufficiently consulted.
Meaningful participation can shape legitimacy, trust, and durable conservation support.

Source: Chapter 4, §4.4.2.


Time: 7 minutes. Use the case facts provided here: designation in 1996 and reduction in 2017. Do not supply external policy details.

title: Justice, Participation, and Governance
section: Diagnose the process, not only the outcome
text:
Diagnose the process, not only the outcome

The case asks more than whether a monument’s boundaries should be larger or smaller.


It asks whose relationships, authority, knowledge, and participation shaped the decision—and what happens when affected communities and Indigenous nations see consultation as insufficient.



Process can affect legitimacy, trust, and the durability of conservation support.



Source: Chapter 4, §4.4.2; Chapter 5, §§5.2–5.3.


Time: 4 minutes. Keep the case chapter-bound. The aim is to help students see why a governance analysis includes both the formal decision and the relationships that give it legitimacy.

title: Justice, Participation, and Governance
text:
Friday preparation: four prompts
Use Chapters 4 and 5 to prepare:

What decision and governance context are described?
What DEIJ concern is visible?
How can consultation shape legitimacy and support?
What participation or collaboration practice could make a decision more durable?


Time: 10 minutes. In pairs, have students locate the relevant case details and identify a governance concept that applies.

title: Justice, Participation, and Governance
section: Pair rehearsal: make one accountable-process claim
text:
Pair rehearsal: make one accountable-process claim
With a partner, complete this claim:

A more durable process would involve ______ early enough to ______. This matters because ______; one constraint or uncertainty is ______.

Use only a participation or collaboration practice described in Chapters 4–5.

Source: Chapters 4–5, §§4.3–4.5 and §§5.2–5.3.


Time: 5 minutes. Give pairs two minutes, hear two claims, then ask the class to name the participation practice and the governance constraint each claim identifies. This is the direct rehearsal for Friday response item 4.

title: Justice, Participation, and Governance
text:
Close: a management standard
Conservation decisions are more durable when they are ecologically sound and publicly accountable to diverse publics, authorities, and contexts.

Source: Chapters 4–5.


Time: 3 minutes. Reiterate Friday’s application source anchors and quiz deadline.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
text:
Today’s question
How do earlier eras of fish and wildlife management still shape a decision made now?


History explains the institutions, funding, laws, professional habits, and public expectations a manager inherits.


Source: Chapter 2, §§2.1–2.2.


Time: 2 minutes. Ask students to name one thing a current agency inherits. Hold examples until the class has a shared vocabulary.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
section: What you should be able to do
text:
What you should be able to do
By the end of today, you should be able to:

identify the defining priority and social context of each historical era;
explain how an earlier era left a legacy for a current decision; and
use a human-dimensions question to examine that legacy rather than treating it as neutral or inevitable.


Source: Chapter 2, guiding questions; §2.2.


Time: 2 minutes. Preview that Wednesday begins with the public-trust question: for whom should inherited institutions act?

title: Conservation History as Living Context
text:
History asks more than “what happened?”



Priority
What problem seemed most urgent?

Context
Which values, economics, and politics shaped the response?

Legacy
What remains in current management?

  

Conservation history traces changing relationships among people, species, habitats, and institutions.


Source: Chapter 2, §§2.1–2.2.


Time: 3 minutes. Use these questions to prevent the class from becoming a list of dates and names.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
text:
Conservation history is cumulative


Source: Chapter 2, Figure 2.1 and §§2.2.1–2.2.8.


Time: 3 minutes. Each layer arose in response to new challenges, but did not erase earlier assumptions or institutions. The figure does not imply equal power across eras.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
section: A timeline tells order; history explains inheritance
text:
A timeline tells order; history explains inheritance



Timeline question
What came next?

Historical question
What did this era leave behind for today’s decisions?

 
An inherited legacy might be a legal framework, a source of agency revenue, an idea about expertise, or a pattern of inclusion and exclusion.

Source: Chapter 2, §2.2.


Time: 2 minutes. Emphasize “left behind,” not simple one-to-one causation.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
section: Indigenous stewardship is the first layer
text:
Indigenous stewardship is the first layer
The history of North American fish and wildlife management begins long before European colonization.

Time: 1 minute. This is a substantive foundation, not a preface to a settler conservation story.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
text:
Indigenous stewardship: reciprocal responsibility
Many Indigenous nations developed place-based stewardship systems over millennia.

Humans are part of relationships with living and nonliving beings.
Stewardship can be guided by respect, relevance, responsibility, and reciprocity.
Knowledge is created and shared across generations through oral and visual traditions.


Source: Chapter 2, §2.2.1.


Time: 3 minutes. Indigenous nations are not monolithic. Contrast this relational framing with the utilitarian resource-or-commodity paradigm later common in Western law and agencies, without treating either tradition as uniform.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
text:
“Pristine wilderness” is an incomplete history
Framing conservation history as beginning with Muir or Roosevelt overlooks the active management of pre-colonial landscapes.

Landscapes were actively shaped by Indigenous peoples: Karuk and Yurok controlled fire; Lakota and Blackfeet developed bison-harvest practices; Lummi and Yakama created salmon fisheries.


Ignoring that stewardship erases Indigenous cultures and can help justify removal from ancestral lands.


Source: Chapter 2, §2.2.1.


Time: 3 minutes. Recognizing this history is both an accuracy and an ethical question.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
text:
The legacy continues through governance
Contemporary collaboration and co-management include:

Mille Lacs Lake fishery management and treaty-rights partners;
Menominee forest management and a seventh-generation responsibility;
Indigenous input to the Alexander Archipelago wolf assessment; and
Hawaiian marine governance that integrates customary values.


Source: Chapter 2, §2.2.1.


Time: 3 minutes. These are not interchangeable models or automatically successful outcomes. The wolf assessment also shows limits in fully incorporating Indigenous knowledge.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
text:
Abundance became a utilitarian premise
1600–1850: European settlers commonly perceived North American resources as effectively endless.

Time: 1 minute. Move to the social and economic premises that made intensive extraction seem reasonable to many settlers.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
section: Era of Abundance: freedom, opportunity, and commodities
text:
Era of Abundance: freedom, opportunity, and commodities
European restrictions on hunting had often served monarchs and aristocrats. In North America, fewer restrictions helped make wildlife seem like:

a freely usable resource;
a symbol of freedom and opportunity; and
a source of profit in market hunting, trapping, and the fur trade.


Perceived abundance helped normalize a belief that use did not require long-term restraint.


Source: Chapter 2, §2.2.2.


Time: 3 minutes. This was a cultural, economic, and political mindset, not merely an error about animal numbers. Use beaver and the global fur trade as the example.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
text:
Exploitation made the limits visible
1850–1900: industrial-scale commerce in “fin, feather, and fur” outpaced weak conservation institutions.

Time: 1 minute. Ask students to listen for a convergence of forces, not a single cause.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
section: Era of Exploitation: short-term use, lasting damage

title: Conservation History as Living Context
section: Bison shows why a social history matters
text:
Bison shows why a social history matters
The near extermination of bison reflected a convergence of:

industrial hide harvest and market demand;
military and government campaigns against Indigenous peoples; and
westward expansion.


Ecological decline is often inseparable from political power, economic systems, and human relationships.


Source: Chapter 2, §2.2.3.


Time: 3 minutes. This is why a purely biological account is incomplete. Keep the claim precise: several forces converged; harvest alone does not explain the outcome.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
text:
Protection changed the rules
1900–1930: overharvest and species decline produced organized advocacy, new laws, and new conservation institutions.

Time: 1 minute. Protection was a response to failure, not a clean break with all earlier social patterns.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
section: Era of Protection: from commodity to public concern
text:
Era of Protection: from commodity to public concern
The passenger pigeon and Carolina parakeet were extinct; bison had fallen to roughly a thousand animals by the 1890s.

Harriet Hemenway and Minna Hall organized opposition to the plume trade and helped establish the Massachusetts Audubon Society.
The Lacey Act (1900) restricted interstate commerce in illegally taken wildlife.


Source: Chapter 2, §2.2.4 and Figure 2.3.


Time: 3 minutes. The plume trade illustrates grassroots advocacy joining government action. Do not reduce the movement to famous figures alone.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
section: Protection required cooperation beyond one state
text:
Protection required cooperation beyond one state
The Migratory Bird Treaty Act (1918):

followed a U.S.–Great Britain treaty acting on Canada’s behalf;
made most migratory birds illegal to hunt, capture, or sell; and
recognized that migratory species require management at a continental scale.


Source: Chapter 2, §2.2.4.


Time: 2 minutes. The instructional point is scale: species cross boundaries that state-by-state rules cannot fully address.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
text:
Game management built a profession
1930–1960: management moved from reactive protection toward proactive, science-based restoration and sustainable use.

Time: 1 minute. Ask what changes when a profession is built around scientific expertise and a dependable revenue source.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
section: Era of Game Management: a durable funding legacy
text:
Era of Game Management: a durable funding legacy









Program
Revenue source
What it supported




Pittman–Robertson Act (1937)
Excise tax on sporting arms and ammunition
State wildlife restoration, habitat, research, public hunting areas


Dingell–Johnson Act (1950)
Excise tax on certain fishing tackle
Sport-fish restoration and related state projects





The model linked purchases by hunters, anglers, and later boaters to public conservation benefits.


Source: Chapter 2, §2.2.5.


Time: 3 minutes. Name the “user-pays, public-benefits” model. Wallop-Breaux later broadened the sport-fish revenue base. Ask how a funding model might shape agency priorities and public expectations.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
text:
Expertise, education, and organizations expanded
Professionalization created a durable infrastructure:

Leopold’s American Game Policy (1930) and Game Management (1933);
a Wisconsin wildlife degree program and Cooperative Wildlife Research Units;
The Wildlife Society and Ducks Unlimited (both 1937); and
a land ethic that framed conservation as a moral duty of care.


Source: Chapter 2, §2.2.5.


Time: 2 minutes. These established scientific principles, credentials, and organizations that still shape practice. Leopold’s land ethic also connects to relational ideas of kinship and reciprocity.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
section: A successful model can still be narrow
text:
A successful model can still be narrow
The game-management era elevated game and sportfish, but it also created costs:

nongame species and broader ecological problems received less priority;
public outreach often remained one-way education; and
programs could displace Indigenous communities, overlook knowledge, and reproduce racial and economic exclusions.


Source: Chapter 2, §2.2.5.


Time: 3 minutes. This is not a dismissal of restoration achievements. Any framework sets priorities and distributes benefits.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
text:
Environmental management broadened the frame
1960–1990: conservation increasingly addressed ecosystems, environmental harm, public participation, and accountability.

Time: 1 minute. The social context included environmental and civil-rights movements, anti-war protest, and increasing distrust of institutions.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
section: Era of Environmental Management: systems, not isolated species
text:
Era of Environmental Management: systems, not isolated species
Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring (1962) helped connect pesticide use to ecological and human-health consequences.

The management question widened: How do habitats, ecosystems, pollution, and human systems interact?


The social question widened too: Who participates, and how are institutions accountable?


Source: Chapter 2, §2.2.6.


Time: 3 minutes. Contrast a priority on selected species and use with an attention to interconnected ecological and human systems. Neither question has disappeared from current practice.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
section: Law made participation and accountability more visible
text:
Law made participation and accountability more visible


National Environmental Policy Act (1970)
Institutionalized public participation and accountability in environmental decision-making.

Endangered Species Act (1973)
Made protection of imperiled species a national conservation priority.


Source: Chapter 2, §2.2.6.


Time: 2 minutes. Keep this out of the weeds of legal procedure. These laws show that conservation is not only a technical question.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
section: Human dimensions became a named professional field
text:
Human dimensions became a named professional field
Early information from hunters often served “surrogate biology”: estimating harvest and population measures.

The emerging field added different questions: landowner–hunter conflict, recreation experiences, wildlife values, economic effects, and public participation.


In 1973, a North American Wildlife and Natural Resources Conference session formally introduced “human dimensions in wildlife programs.”


Source: Chapter 2, §2.2.6, Boxes 2.1–2.2.


Time: 3 minutes. Data collected from people are not automatically human-dimensions research; the management question and purpose matter. Give Missouri’s early farmer/hunter studies and the 1955 National Survey as chapter examples.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
section: Institutionalization changed who agencies could learn from
text:
Institutionalization changed who agencies could learn from








Development
What it made more possible




Missouri hired Dan Witter (1978)
Full-time agency human-dimensions expertise


Cornell’s Human Dimensions Research Unit
Dedicated university research capacity


Yale’s Human Dimensions of Wildlife Study Group
Professional scholarly community


Later journals and university programs
A recognized field and shared methods





Source: Chapter 2, §2.2.6, Boxes 2.1–2.2.


Time: 2 minutes. Agency leadership and university research both mattered. The “N of 1” capacity challenge returns in modern challenges.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
section: Globalization and international governance change the scale
text:
Globalization and international governance change the scale
1990–present: conservation problems and solutions increasingly cross ecological, political, and social boundaries.

Time: 1 minute. This is another layer, not a replacement for local or state management.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
text:
Global challenges require connected governance
Contemporary conservation faces interconnected challenges:

biodiversity loss and landscape fragmentation;
wildlife trade and invasive species;
climate change and shifting species distributions; and
urbanization and changing relationships with wildlife.


When a problem crosses boundaries, management needs cooperation among institutions, communities, and publics at multiple scales.


Source: Chapter 2, §2.2.7.


Time: 2 minutes. Give the North American Waterfowl Management Plan as a cross-border partnership example.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
text:
International frameworks meet local knowledge
Global agreements and local governance operate together:

CBD and CITES help align national and local work with global priorities.
The European Union’s Common Fisheries Policy uses public engagement and adaptive management.
Namibia’s community conservancies connect local knowledge, livelihoods, wildlife coexistence, and conservation goals.


Source: Chapter 2, §2.2.7.


Time: 3 minutes. Treat the examples as illustrations, not blueprints. In Namibia, tourism and regulated-hunting income can be reinvested in local projects, potentially reducing conflict and supporting conservation.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
section: Modern challenges reveal the accumulated layers
text:
Modern challenges reveal the accumulated layers
The history becomes useful when it helps diagnose a present conservation problem.

Time: 1 minute. Shift from historical description to application.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
section: A present decision is social, ecological, and institutional
text:
A present decision is social, ecological, and institutional
For urban wildlife, predator reintroduction, habitat restoration, or climate adaptation, a manager may need to ask:

Which publics experience benefits, costs, or risk?
Which authorities and knowledge systems have a role?
What history shapes funding, trust, access, or participation?
What new challenges make older approaches insufficient?


Source: Chapter 2, §2.2.8.


Time: 3 minutes. Ground these in wildlife conflict, rural/urban tension, Tribal/state/federal authority, technology, justice, capacity, nonconsumptive use, and changing societal values.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
text:
Technology adds capacity—and new questions


New possibilities
GIS, remote sensing, data science, iNaturalist, eBird, and social media can expand research and participation.

New responsibilities
Managers must consider access, data quality, privacy, misinformation, and who benefits from technology.


Source: Chapter 2, §2.2.8.


Time: 2 minutes. Technology is not only a tool; it changes relationships, authority, participation, and distribution of benefits.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
text:
Practice: trace one legacy forward
With a partner, choose one Chapter 2 era. Prepare a 45-second explanation:

What priority, institution, or assumption is associated with that era?
How could it still shape a current fish or wildlife decision?
What human-dimensions question would a manager ask before treating that legacy as neutral or inevitable?


Source: Chapter 2, §2.2.


Time: 7 minutes. Give pairs 3 minutes to prepare, then hear three explanations and compare them. Prompt for specificity: “funding from excise taxes” is stronger than “the past matters.”

title: Conservation History as Living Context
text:
From history to public responsibility

History shows that management inherits layered priorities and institutions.


Wednesday asks the next question:

For whom should those institutions act, and how are they accountable?



Source: Chapter 2, §§2.2–2.3; Chapter 3, §§3.1–3.3.


Time: 2 minutes. Connect to public trust thinking: beneficiaries, trustees, trust managers, and future generations.

title: Conservation History as Living Context
text:
Exit check
Complete both statements:

One current management decision is shaped by the legacy of ______ because ______.
A human-dimensions question about that legacy would ask ______.


Source: Chapter 2, §§2.2–2.3.


Time: 3 minutes. Look for an era-specific claim and an actual management connection: values, publics, institutions, participation, funding, authority, access, or distribution of benefits and burdens.

title: NRES 315: Course Launch
text:
Welcome to NRES 315
This course examines the human actions, social processes, and social-ecological relationships that shape fish and wildlife management.
Today is a brief launch. Wednesday is our full Chapter 1 session.

Course framing: Chapter 1, §1.3. Schedule: course syllabus.


Time: 2 minutes. Welcome students and establish that today is an orientation, not an abbreviated version of Wednesday’s lecture.

title: NRES 315: Course Launch
text:
The recurring course question
Fish and wildlife management decisions involve people, habitats, and species.
Across the semester, we will ask:

What decision is being made, what evidence matters, who is affected, and which tradeoffs must be addressed?


Chapter 1 framing: §§1.2.1–1.3.


Time: 3 minutes. This is the course’s recurring reasoning routine. Do not unpack the terms fully yet; Wednesday’s Chapter 1 lecture will do that.

title: NRES 315: Course Launch
text:
How our weeks work











Monday
Wednesday
Friday




Frame the chapter and management question
Lecture, concept check, and case preparation
Rotating small-group application


Complete reading preparation
Bring one claim and one question
Submit one shared response and a private Friday Group Check






Source: course syllabus, “Weekly rhythm.”


Time: 4 minutes. Explain that the weekly pattern is predictable. In Week 1, Monday is shorter and Wednesday carries the chapter framing. Friday is the first graded application; from Week 2 onward, groups rotate weekly.

title: NRES 315: Course Launch
text:
How the course is assessed

Reading quizzes — 25%: short, individual preparation checks; the lowest one score is dropped.
Weekly group applications — 75%: fifteen in-class applications; the lowest one score is dropped.
Each application score is 80% shared reasoning and 20% individual contribution accountability.


Source: course syllabus, “Assessment and grading.”


Time: 3 minutes. Emphasize the point of the structure: prepare individually, reason with others in class, and show meaningful contribution. Mention that there are no unit exams or cumulative final exam.

title: NRES 315: Course Launch
text:
Your Week 1 checklist

Find the Week 1 module in Canvas.
Read Chapter 1.
Complete the individual quiz by Sunday, August 30, at 11:59 p.m., before Week 02 Monday class.
Come Wednesday ready to discuss one management question from the chapter.
Come Friday ready for the first graded Chesapeake Bay application.


Source: Week 1 Canvas module and Chapter 1.


Time: 4 minutes. Direct students to the blank Canvas course’s Week 1 module once published. Be explicit that the Friday exercise uses the shared-response and private Friday Group Check routines; it is graded.

title: NRES 315: Course Launch
section: A question to carry into Wednesday
text:
A question to carry into Wednesday
Chapter 1 argues that biology and ecology are essential—but cannot independently determine:

which goals should be pursued;
which tradeoffs are acceptable; or
who should participate.

Write down one fish or wildlife decision for which you think one of those questions would matter.

Source: Chapter 1, §§1.2–1.2.1.


Time: 3 minutes. Give one quiet minute to write, then invite two short examples. Do not answer or evaluate them in depth; collect the question and use it as the bridge to Wednesday.

title: NRES 315: Course Launch
text:
Wednesday begins Chapter 1 in full
Bring your Chapter 1 question back on Wednesday.
We will work through values and actions, people–habitats–species, research and participation, and the everyday work of human dimensions.

Source: Chapter 1, §§1.2–1.5.


Time: 1 minute. Close clearly: read Chapter 1, complete the quiz by Sunday night, and return Wednesday ready to use the chapter’s full argument.

title: NRES 315: People, Habitats, and Species
text:
Today’s question
When biological evidence is sound, what still has to be worked out before a fish or wildlife decision can succeed?

Source: Chapter 1, guiding questions; §§1.2–1.5.


Time: 2 minutes. Frame this as the chapter’s central question, not as an argument against biological science. Invite one or two initial responses without resolving them yet.

title: NRES 315: People, Habitats, and Species
section: What you should be able to do
text:
What you should be able to do
By the end of today, you should be able to:

explain why management is value-laden;
use human dimensions as a problem orientation, not merely a set of public-opinion tools;
distinguish research, participation, and transdisciplinary collaboration; and
identify the human work embedded in a conservation decision.


Source: Chapter 1, guiding questions and §§1.2–1.5.


Time: 1 minute. These objectives follow the chapter’s guiding questions. Tell students that Friday’s practice will use the Chesapeake Bay example from this chapter.

title: NRES 315: People, Habitats, and Species
section: Chesapeake Bay is a shared social–ecological system
text:
Chesapeake Bay is a shared social–ecological system



The Bay is degraded by overfishing, pollution, nutrient loading, and habitat destruction.

Runoff from agricultural and urban areas contributes to seasonal low-oxygen “dead zones.”
Underwater grass beds and oyster reefs have declined, reducing nursery habitat for fishery species.
Restoration decisions affect fisheries, livelihoods, recreation, and a place with deep cultural and Indigenous significance.






Instructional content: Chapter 1, §1.2. Illustrative image: Steve Adams / Unsplash.


Time: 2 minutes. Establish the Bay as the chapter’s recurring example. The point is not to memorize its facts; it is to see a management problem as an ecological system and a working landscape.

title: NRES 315: People, Habitats, and Species
section: The same Bay contains different stakes
text:
The same Bay contains different stakes
Different publics may agree that the Bay matters while disagreeing about the problem, its causes, and acceptable solutions.

Commercial fishers may focus on livelihood effects.
Recreational anglers may emphasize fish abundance, clean water, and access.
Farmers and landowners may face new runoff or conservation expectations.
Environmental organizations may seek stricter standards.


Source: Chapter 1, §1.2.


Time: 2 minutes. Ask: “Does naming all of these interests decide what to do?” No. It makes the management problem more accurately visible. Avoid turning these groups into caricatures.

title: NRES 315: People, Habitats, and Species
section: Diagnosing the Bay is not the same as deciding what to do
text:
Diagnosing the Bay is not the same as deciding what to do

Ecological science identifies the Bay’s condition and the likely effects of actions. It does not choose the action.


Science can clarify

nutrient inputs, water quality, and habitat condition;
likely effects of management actions.


A decision must still address

priority outcomes;
acceptable tradeoffs; and
affected publics and costs.



Ecological evidence identifies choices; values shape which choice is pursued.



Source: Chapter 1, §§1.2–1.2.1.


Time: 2 minutes. Use the two columns as the handoff. First, ecological evidence identifies the condition and likely effects of options. Then ask: “Once we know that, what tells us which option to pursue?” The next slide names the answer: values shape the outcomes and actions people support.

title: NRES 315: People, Habitats, and Species
section: Management is an expression of human values and actions
text:
Management is an expression of human values and actions
Management and conservation are value-laden enterprises.


A value is a belief that an action—or the end state it produces—is desirable.
Values shape the outcomes people prefer for fish, wildlife, and habitats.
Values also shape the actions and policies people support to reach those outcomes.
Because values differ, management choices can create conflict and tradeoffs.



Source: Chapter 1, §1.2.1, “Human Values Are Fish and Wildlife Management.”


Time: 3 minutes. Use the chapter’s sequence: What end state is preferred for a species—protection, conservation, or hunting—and which actions are thought to lead there? Do not collapse the chapter’s distinctions among instrumental/intrinsic, anthropocentric/biological, or utilitarian/mutualistic values; flag them as later vocabulary.

title: NRES 315: People, Habitats, and Species
section: Decisions are nested within people, habitats, and species
text:
Decisions are nested within people, habitats, and species


Source: Chapter 1, Figure 1.1 and §1.2.1.


Time: 3 minutes. The published chapter caption calls this the three-legged-stool model; use the figure as a visible synthesis. Habitats and species draw heavily on biological and ecological sciences; the people dimension draws on social science, governance, and engagement. A stable decision integrates all three.

title: NRES 315: People, Habitats, and Species
section: People and Natural Resources Affect Each Other
text:
People and Natural Resources Affect Each Other
Human dimensions concerns the human actions, social processes, and social-ecological relationships that shape management.

People affect fish, wildlife, and habitats through development, agriculture, harvest, recreation, and extraction.
Fish, wildlife, and habitats affect people through subsistence, livelihoods, meanings, places, and other benefits.
Those relationships shape management decisions.


Source: Chapter 1, §1.3.


Time: 2 minutes. Emphasize reciprocity. HD is not a late-stage communication task after a biological decision is made; it describes relationships that are already shaping the system and the decision.

title: NRES 315: People, Habitats, and Species
section: Human dimensions broadens the questions we ask
text:
Human dimensions broadens the questions we ask
For a deer season structure, biological analysis might ask:

How will the population change?
What harvest level is sustainable?
Are population goals being met?

A human dimensions orientation also asks:

How will hunters respond to the season structure?
How might it affect satisfaction, crowding, access, safety, or local economies?
Who is affected, and what values may be in conflict?
What evidence and public participation are needed?


Source: Chapter 1, §1.3.


Time: 3 minutes. This is the chapter’s deer-season example. Explain that human and biological evidence together improve the chances of decisions that can be implemented and publicly supported; neither is a substitute for the other.

title: NRES 315: People, Habitats, and Species
text:
Two complementary ways of working


Source: Chapter 1, Figure 1.2 and §1.3.


Time: 3 minutes. Keep the two columns distinct. Research investigates; participation includes publics and beneficiaries in governance, planning, and decisions. Professional judgment and lived experience remain part of the broader HD practice described in the text.

title: NRES 315: People, Habitats, and Species
section: Research asks systematic questions about people
text:
Research asks systematic questions about people

The social sciences provide principles, theories, methods, standards, and criteria for rigor.
They help professionals describe and explain human values, attitudes, behaviors, institutions, causes, and outcomes—and critically examine assumptions and biases.

 

“Social science” is not one expertise. Psychology, sociology, anthropology, economics, law, policy science, political ecology, and environmental humanities bring different tools.


Source: Chapter 1, §1.3.1 and Table 1.1.


Time: 2 minutes. Use the chapter’s analogy: an entomologist and mammalogist are not interchangeable, nor are a sociologist and political scientist. This is why transdisciplinary work needs specific expertise rather than a generic “social science” box.

title: NRES 315: People, Habitats, and Species
text:
Participation has two related forms
 










Public involvement
Engagement




Formal and legally required within a planning or decision process
Continual interaction and dialogue with publics


Includes notice, opportunity to participate, and a record of decision
Emphasizes shared learning, relationship-building, and trust


Example: notice-and-comment rulemaking
Example: an advisory group, community event, extension, or outreach






Source: Chapter 1, §1.3.2.


Time: 3 minutes. This is an important nuance. Do not imply that engagement is legally optional and therefore unimportant; the chapter presents it as a sustained practice that can make management more effective and trustworthy.

title: NRES 315: People, Habitats, and Species
section: Collaboration is more than assembling experts
text:
Collaboration is more than assembling experts
Transdisciplinary work goes beyond assembling academic expertise: it includes non-academic partners in defining the problem and producing useful knowledge.



Source: Chapter 1, §1.3.3.


Time: 2 minutes. Read the diagram left to right. The key distinction is that transdisciplinary work does not merely integrate academic fields; non-academic partners jointly orient the problem and produce knowledge. Connect this to questions such as predator management, anadromous fish conservation, Tribal sovereignty and treaty rights, and access disputes, where the chapter says participation, deliberation, trust, lived experience, and Indigenous knowledge may all matter.

title: NRES 315: People, Habitats, and Species
text:
Collaboration requires understanding different perspectives
Working with publics means recognizing that people may understand the same problem very differently.
Their perspectives are shaped by:

values, beliefs, and attitudes
norms and direct experiences
risk perceptions and satisfaction
political, historical, and cultural context

Human dimensions helps make these differences visible and asks:

Will different publics experience the decision as fair, legitimate, and acceptable?


Source: Chapter 1, §1.4.1.


Time: 2 minutes. Explain that systematic research, principled participation, and multiple knowledge systems help professionals align ecological goals with social realities. This is not a promise that all publics will agree.

title: NRES 315: People, Habitats, and Species
section: Different perspectives can create conflict—and exclusion
text:
Different perspectives can create conflict—and exclusion



Human–wildlife interactions are rarely solved by technical fixes alone.
Lasting responses may require:

dialogue among people with different interests and values;
trust in agencies, processes, and other participants; and
meaningful participation by affected publics.




Human dimensions also asks:
Who gets to participate—and who bears the costs of conservation decisions?



Instructional content: Chapter 1, §§1.4.2–1.4.3. Illustrative image: Emmanuel Munoz / Unsplash.


Time: 2 minutes. Use chapter examples sparingly: elk and agricultural losses, mountain lions and livestock, urban raccoons and property damage. Then make explicit that the chapter identifies Indigenous peoples, racial and ethnic minorities, economically disadvantaged groups, and some rural populations as facing barriers to participation or disproportionate burdens. Indigenous leadership, traditional knowledge, community-led restoration, mentorship, and removing financial or logistical barriers can strengthen both justice and conservation relevance.

title: NRES 315: People, Habitats, and Species
section: Management decisions happen in the real world
text:
Management decisions happen in the real world

Natural resource professionals work within changing social, political, economic, and environmental conditions.
That means navigating:

politics and resources — political influence, budgets, development, and competing uses;
trust and communication — misinformation, public trust, and shared responsibility;
technology — new opportunities for research and access, alongside ethical and equity concerns; and
large-scale change — climate change and urbanization that require engagement, incentives, and collaboration.



Good science is necessary—but it does not determine what is feasible, acceptable, or durable.


Source: Chapter 1, §§1.4.4–1.4.7.


Time: 2 minutes. This is the chapter’s final practice arc, not a miscellaneous list. Link economics to policy impacts and nonmarket values; policy analysis to power and institutional structures; digital engagement to both access and digital exclusion; and climate adaptation to implementation with governments, communities, and conservation organizations.

title: NRES 315: People, Habitats, and Species
text:
Practice: reframe Chesapeake Bay restoration
In groups, use only the Chapter 1 account of the Bay. Prepare a 60-second explanation that answers:

What is the ecological condition or management concern?
Whose values, actions, or responsibilities make this a human-dimensions problem?
What is one research need and one participation need before a durable decision?


Source: Chapter 1, §§1.2–1.3.3.


Time: 7 minutes. Give groups 3 minutes to prepare, hear two 60-second responses, then use 2 minutes to compare their research and participation choices. This prepares students for Friday’s first graded application.

title: NRES 315: People, Habitats, and Species
section: Effective management has a wider standard

title: NRES 315: People, Habitats, and Species
text:
From Wednesday to Friday
For Friday’s graded Chesapeake Bay application:

make people, habitats, and species visible;
identify two affected publics and a tradeoff; and
distinguish evidence needed from participation needed.

The Week 1 reading quiz is due Sunday, August 30, at 11:59 p.m., before Week 02 Monday class.

Source: Chapter 1, §§1.2–1.3.3; Week 1 Canvas module.


Time: 1 minute. Connect the week’s sequence to the Canvas page. Do not add case facts beyond Chapter 1.

title: NRES 315: People, Habitats, and Species
text:
Exit check
Complete both statements:

Biological evidence cannot by itself decide ______.
A human-dimensions problem orientation changes a decision by asking ______.


Source: Chapter 1, §§1.2.1, 1.3, and 1.5.


Time: 1 minute. Use a written or verbal response. Listen for values/tradeoffs/affected publics/participation and the reciprocal connection among people, habitats, and species.

title: Public Trust: For Whom and For What?
text:
Today’s question
What does it mean to manage fish and wildlife as a public trust?

Source: Chapter 3, §3.1–3.2.


Time: 3 minutes. Retrieve the Week 2 Monday question: How does history shape present management?

title: Public Trust: For Whom and For What?
section: What you should be able to do
text:
What you should be able to do
By the end of today, you should be able to:

distinguish public trust thinking from the public trust doctrine;
identify assets, beneficiaries, trustees, and trust managers in a management problem; and
explain why accountability to current and future publics matters for a defensible decision.


Source: Chapter 3, §§3.1–3.4.


Time: 2 minutes. Preview that the Friday case asks students to use these terms, not only recognize them.

title: Public Trust: For Whom and For What?
text:
A public responsibility
Fish and wildlife management asks not only what works, but for whom it must work.

Time: 1 minute. Use this as a bridge from Monday’s historical inheritance to Chapter 3’s present responsibility.

title: Public Trust: For Whom and For What?
text:
The public-trust starting point
Free-ranging fish and wildlife are generally treated as public resources rather than objects of private ownership.

Public trust thinking asks managers to steward these resources for current and future publics.


Source: Chapter 3, §3.2.


Time: 5 minutes. Explain that this is a philosophical and practical framework, not merely a slogan.

title: Public Trust: For Whom and For What?
section: An endowment, not a private commodity
text:
An endowment, not a private commodity
Public trust thinking begins from three linked claims:

fish and wildlife are an endowment held across generations;
their benefits deserve fair consideration for all citizens; and
government has a stewardship responsibility that cannot be reduced to serving one present-day user group.


Source: Chapter 3, §§3.2–3.3 and Table 3.1.


Time: 3 minutes. Connect this to Monday: the legal and institutional layers of conservation are inherited, but public trust thinking asks what present responsibility they create. Do not equate fair consideration with identical outcomes for every public.

title: Public Trust: For Whom and For What?
text:
Core public-trust questions

What are the trust assets?
Who are the beneficiaries?
Who acts as trustee, trust manager, or trust administrator?
How are current and future generations considered?
How can beneficiaries hold administrators accountable?


Source: Chapter 3, §3.1–3.3.


Time: 7 minutes. Use these terms precisely. Students will use them Friday.

title: Public Trust: For Whom and For What?
text:
A trust has connected roles


Assets
Fish and wildlife within a government’s jurisdiction.

Beneficiaries
Current and future publics with legitimate interests in how assets are managed.

Trust administrators
Trustees make public decisions; trust managers carry out daily professional work.


The public-trust question is relational: who is responsible to whom, for what, and across what time horizon?


Source: Chapter 3, §§3.3.1–3.3.3.


Time: 5 minutes. Clarify that beneficiaries are broader than the loudest or most direct users. Trustees are elected or appointed officials with decision authority; trust managers are professional civil servants responsible for implementation and communication.

title: Public Trust: For Whom and For What?
section: Trustees and trust managers do different work
text:
Trustees and trust managers do different work


Trustees
Public officials who set direction, make decisions, and are accountable to beneficiaries.

Trust managers
Professional staff who develop options, implement decisions, communicate, and learn from results.


Authority and expertise are connected, but they are not interchangeable.


Source: Chapter 3, §3.3.3.


Time: 3 minutes. Ask students which role they would expect to set a harvest regulation and which role would collect evidence or communicate implementation. A manager can advise and implement without possessing the same legal authority as a trustee.

title: Public Trust: For Whom and For What?
text:
Intergenerational equity
Present generations have responsibilities to steward resources so that current choices do not foreclose important future options.

Source: Chapter 3, §3.2.


Time: 5 minutes. Ask students what makes this more demanding than simply serving current users. Do not introduce extra examples.

title: Public Trust: For Whom and For What?
section: Intergenerational equity changes the time horizon
text:
Intergenerational equity changes the time horizon


A narrow present-only question
Who gains or loses from this decision now?

A public-trust question
What options, resources, and responsibilities will this decision leave for future beneficiaries?


Source: Chapter 3, §3.2.


Time: 2 minutes. This is not a promise that every future outcome can be predicted. It is a duty to make the time horizon visible rather than treating it as irrelevant.

title: Public Trust: For Whom and For What?
text:
Accountability is part of stewardship

Trust administrators need to explain what information they considered, how public input was used, and why a decision was made.


Transparency does not guarantee agreement.


It gives beneficiaries a basis to understand and evaluate whether administrators are serving the public interest.


Source: Chapter 3, §3.4.


Time: 4 minutes. Distinguish accountability from unanimity. This is the bridge from the framework to human-dimensions research and participation.

title: Public Trust: For Whom and For What?
text:
Public trust thinking and doctrine

Public trust thinking guides law, policy, and practice; the doctrine is one legal expression of that responsibility.

Source: Chapter 3, §3.2–3.3.


Time: 6 minutes. Use the figure’s alt text as the text equivalent. Ask students to make the distinction in their own words before revealing the final sentence.

title: Public Trust: For Whom and For What?
section: Doctrine is one tool within a broader responsibility
text:
Doctrine is one tool within a broader responsibility
Public trust thinking is the broader philosophical and practical orientation for stewardship.
Public trust doctrine is a legal concept that can define or protect public interests in particular settings.

Legal compliance matters, but it does not exhaust the question of whether a decision serves current and future beneficiaries well.


Source: Chapter 3, §§3.3.4–3.4.


Time: 3 minutes. This distinction is essential for Friday. Students should avoid saying every public-trust question has a single doctrine-based answer.

title: Public Trust: For Whom and For What?
text:
From framework to case
The Montana stream-access conflict asks how public responsibility works when water and private property interests meet.

Time: 1 minute. Tell students that the case does not ask them to settle a general property-law debate; it asks them to analyze a specific public-access conflict accurately.

title: Public Trust: For Whom and For What?
text:
Friday application: Montana stream access
The Montana stream-access conflict asks whether public use of water can be protected when adjacent landowners claim control of a riverbed or bank.

Dearborn River and Beaverhead River conflicts
Curran and Hildreth
navigability for title versus navigability for use
Montana Stream Access Law


Source: Chapter 3, §3.5.1.


Time: 8 minutes. This is a concise case preview. Students should reread §3.5.1 before Friday; do not use facts beyond it.

title: Public Trust: For Whom and For What?
text:
Case-preparation pair work
With a partner, prepare four labels for Friday:

asset;
beneficiaries;
authority and accountability; and
the boundary on public access in the Montana case.


Time: 10 minutes. Require students to locate support in §3.5.1, then cold-call two pairs for one label each.

title: Public Trust: For Whom and For What?
text:
Practice the distinction before Friday
Complete this sentence with a partner:

Navigability for title asks ______; navigability for use asks ______.

Then add: why did that distinction matter for public access in Montana?

Source: Chapter 3, §3.5.1.


Time: 4 minutes. Give pairs one minute to formulate the distinction, then have two pairs share. The expected contrast is ownership of land beneath water versus whether the public may use water for recreation. Keep the discussion within the facts provided for this case.

title: Public Trust: For Whom and For What?
text:
Close: a defensible public-trust answer
A defensible answer does more than name a law. It explains how assets, beneficiaries, authority, and accountability relate to an actual management conflict.

Source: Chapter 3, §3.5.


Time: 4 minutes. Remind students: the next reading quiz is due Sunday at 11:59 p.m. before Monday’s class; Friday applies these concepts to the Montana case.

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
text:
Building from Week 3
Last week: Legitimate conservation decisions require attention to justice, participation, and governance.
This week: How do managers use evidence to plan, act, and learn?

Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, §§6.1–6.2. Retrieve the prior connection: authority and participation shape which problems are recognized and whose evidence counts.


Source: Chapter 6, §§6.1–6.2

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
text:
The central question

How does a human-dimensions orientation improve an evidence-based management decision?


It broadens both the evidence managers use and the outcomes they seek.


Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, §§6.1–6.2. Ask students to listen for two threads today: evidence and problem framing.


Source: Chapter 6, §§6.1–6.2

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
text:
Evidence and framing
From a management question to a defensible plan.

Time: 1 minute. Transition slide.

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
section: A decision needs more than biological evidence
text:
A decision needs more than biological evidence


What is happening?

Biological or ecological conditions
Technical feasibility
Legal mandates


What should be done?

Economic feasibility
Social values
Public knowledge and experience



Key point: These evidence sources complement one another; none resolves every management question alone.


Time: 6 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, §6.2.1. Emphasize balance rather than a hierarchy of evidence.


Source: Chapter 6, §6.2.1

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
section: Evidence answers different parts of the decision
text:
Evidence answers different parts of the decision








Evidence type
A question it can help answer




Ecological and biological
What condition, risk, or response is occurring?


Social and economic
Who is affected, what matters, and what tradeoffs are feasible?


Legal and institutional
What authority, duty, or process applies?


Local and experiential
What place-based knowledge or implementation concern should shape the plan?





Source: Chapter 6, §6.2.1.


Time: 3 minutes. Evidence types answer different questions; the table does not create a hierarchy or claim each source resolves a decision alone.

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
text:
Four questions organize a decision


Why?
Why manage or conserve this resource?
Who?
Which publics, beneficiaries, and partners are involved?

What?
What impacts or outcomes are desired?
How?
How will the decision be made, carried out, and assessed?


Time: 6 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, §6.2. Ask students which question is easiest to overlook when a decision is framed only as a biological problem.


Source: Chapter 6, §6.2

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
section: Research and participation have different jobs
text:
Research and participation have different jobs
Research can describe conditions, relationships, and likely consequences.
Participation can reveal values, concerns, local knowledge, and acceptable tradeoffs.


Meaningful participation is more than a legal requirement. It needs a structured process, capable staff, and genuine integration of input.



Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, §6.2.1. Connect to Grand Staircase–Escalante: participation affects both information and legitimacy.


Source: Chapter 6, §6.2.1

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
text:
Evidence-informed does not mean expert-only
Research can reduce uncertainty and test relationships. Participation can clarify values, lived experience, local knowledge, and acceptable tradeoffs.

A defensible process makes both the evidence considered and the role of public input visible.


Source: Chapter 6, §6.2.1.


Time: 2 minutes. Connect this to Chapters 3–5: public participation and accountability are part of sound decision processes, not extras after a technically complete decision.

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
text:
Plan–Do–Learn is iterative


Learning can revise the action, the objectives, or even the original problem frame.


Time: 6 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, §6.3 and Figure 6.1. Explain the image in words before discussing it. The alt text provides the text equivalent.

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
section: Structured decision making makes choices inspectable
text:
Structured decision making makes choices inspectable
Structured decision making makes the links explicit among:

the decision context and problem;
objectives and measurable outcomes;
management alternatives; and
predicted consequences, tradeoffs, and uncertainty.


Source: Chapter 6, §6.3.1.


Time: 3 minutes. The goal is not to make every decision slow or overly technical. It is to make the reasoning visible enough to compare alternatives and learn from results.

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
section: Planning turns a broad concern into a choice
text:
Planning turns a broad concern into a choice
Clear framing, objectives, alternatives, and measures.

Time: 1 minute. Transition slide.

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
section: Problem framing shapes the whole cycle
text:
Problem framing shapes the whole cycle
How a problem is framed influences:

who is involved;
what evidence is gathered;
which alternatives are considered; and
how success is measured.


Different frames can produce different, defensible management choices.


Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, §§6.3–6.4. Have students apply why/who/what/how to the Puget Sound effort as a low-stakes preview.


Source: Chapter 6, §§6.3–6.4

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
section: A goal gives direction; objectives make it testable
text:
A goal gives direction; objectives make it testable


Goal
A broad, desired direction for management.

Objective
A specific, measurable statement of what the plan intends to achieve.


Source: Chapter 6, §6.3.2.1.


Time: 2 minutes. Students often jump directly from a broad concern to an action. This distinction makes the missing middle visible.

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
section: Objectives, actions, and measures are not interchangeable
text:
Objectives, actions, and measures are not interchangeable


Objective
The desired change.
Example: Improve access.

Action
What managers do.
Example: Restore a boat ramp.

Measure
Evidence of change.
Example: Reported ability to access the site.


SMART objectives are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound.


Time: 7 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, §§6.3.2–6.3.2.2. Use the example only to distinguish the three terms; do not treat it as a Chapter 6 case claim.


Source: Chapter 6, §§6.3.2–6.3.2.2

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
section: A success metric should support a management decision
text:
A success metric should support a management decision
A useful metric is not merely easy to count. It should be:

connected to an objective;
sensitive enough to detect meaningful change;
feasible to collect and interpret; and
useful for choosing whether to continue, adjust, or replace an action.


Source: Chapter 6, §6.3.2.2.


Time: 3 minutes. A metric is part of the learning system. Ask what would be lost if a plan monitored only activity—such as number of meetings or dollars spent—rather than outcomes.

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
section: “Do” includes implementation, not just a decision
text:
“Do” includes implementation, not just a decision
Once an alternative is chosen, professionals must translate it into action through roles, resources, communication, partnerships, and attention to implementation conditions.

Source: Chapter 6, §6.3.3.


Time: 2 minutes. Bring forward the governance link: an action can be technically attractive but infeasible without authority, funding, partners, or an implementation plan.

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
text:
“Learn” requires monitoring and evaluation


Monitor
Collect information about conditions, implementation, and outcomes over time.

Evaluate
Interpret that information against objectives to decide what should change.


Learning can change an action, an objective, or the original problem frame.


Source: Chapter 6, §§6.3.4–6.3.4.2.


Time: 3 minutes. Monitoring alone is not learning. Evaluation connects observations to a decision about whether to continue or adapt.

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
text:
Preparing for Friday: Puget Sound
Puget Sound’s long-term recovery effort considers ecological conditions and human well-being together.

Come Friday ready to identify:

the why, who, what, and how;
one kind of evidence that matters; and
one outcome worth monitoring.



Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, Box 6.2. Preview only; Wednesday will develop implementation, monitoring, and the Human Well-being Vital Signs.

title: Evidence, Framing, and Planning
text:
Exit check
An agency relies only on biological information to choose an action.
Which of the four decision questions is most likely to be weakened—and why?

Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 6, §6.2. Collect a short written response or pair-share. Close by previewing the Plan–Do–Learn cycle for Wednesday.


Source: Chapter 6, §6.2
